newsitem.title: USA: Hughes buy raises Raytheon debt to $11 billion.
newsitem.headline: Hughes buy raises Raytheon debt to $11 billion.

text.p: Raytheon Co. said Friday its debt will balloon to $11 billion upon completion of its recent defence takeovers, but the missile and radar giant expects to be able to pay down most of that debt over seven years.

Raytheon raised its debt levels to $11 billion from just $3.6 billion earlier this month with two major takeovers of missile and radar rivals, placing it among the top three defence companies in the industry.

Lexington, Mass.-based Raytheon will assume $4.4 billion in debt as part of the proposed stock-and-debt takeover of Hughes Aircraft from General Motors Corp. for $9.5 billion that was announced Thursday.
The defence giant added about $3 billion in debt from its proposed cash takeover of the defence assets of Texas Instruments Inc. on Jan. 6.

Raytheon Chief Financial Officer Peter D'Angelo told reporters Friday the company has a seven-year plan to cut that debt by $7 billion, and analysts speculated the company may sell or spin off some assets.
"Our projections indicate that over a seven-year period we'll be able to pay down ... approximately $7 billion in debt," he said during a conference call.
As part of that plan, Raytheon will borrow about $1 billion in its 30-year debt and around $3.5 billion in debt maturing in two to 10 years, he said.
D'Angelo said the Hughes deal would dilute Raytheon's per share earnings by "single digits" this year, add about 1 percent to earnings in 1998 and about 7 percent in 1999.
But he said the price and short-term impact on earnings was well worth it to create a $21 billion company.
"We have said all along that we intend to remain a top-tier player in defence, and these two recent transactions firmly estabilish our leadership position in the industry."

As part of the deal, Raytheon said Friday three members of its 15-member board of directors will step down, to be replaced by two executives of Hughes Aircraft and one from Hughes Aircrafts' former parent, General Motors Corp.
Raytheon will take a "hard look" at all its assets, and try to unlock the "trapped value" of some of its commercial businesses, he said.

Analysts said because Raytheon also has multibillion-dollar units in the engineering and construction, home appliance and aircraft industries, Wall Street has a difficult time putting a proper value on those units and thus Raytheon's shares may be undervalued.

The investment community has reasoned a $644 million initial public offering by Gulfstream Aerospace Corp. last September unlocked its trapped value and that perhaps Raytheon could do the same with its Beech aircraft division, D'Angelo said. However, he declined to say whether Raytheon was considering such a move.

"I don't think they are going to sell Beech," analyst Cai Von Rumohr of brokerage Cowen & Co. said. "I think they can sell (Amana) appliances, they might sell some of their commercial electronic operations. They can sell (Amana) without diluting their earnings.

Von Rumohr upgraded his recommendation on Raytheon to a buy from neutral Friday. He said Raytheon is generating a healthy cash flow and has sufficient capacity to borrow so that the debt levels do not worry him.
Raytheon rose 25 cents to $48.75 Friday on the New York Stock Exchange.
